[exc_dd1e65de648fb2_998_v2] Learning Statistics with R — Statistical tools › 15 Linear regression › 15.2 Estimating a linear regression model › 15.2.1 Using the lm() function (pages 610)
roles: formal, worked_example | topics: using-r, linear-regression, estimation
teaches: Shows how to fit a simple linear regression in R with lm(formula, data), using danielle_grump as the outcome and danielle_sleep as the sole predictor.
scope: R-specific simple linear regression with an intercept and one predictor. The coefficient interpretation continues in the next excerpt. It does not teach multiple regression.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_dd1e65de648fb2_999_v2
As we saw with aov() in Comparing several means (one-way ANOVA), the output of the lm() function is a fairly complicated object, with quite a lot of technical information buried under the hood. Because this technical information is used by other functions, it’s generally a good idea to create a variable that stores the results of your regression. With this in mind, to run my linear regression, the command I want to use is this:

regression_1 <- lm( formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood

)

Note that I used danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep as the formula: in the model that I’m trying to estimate, danielle_grump is the outcome variable, and danielle_sleep is the predictor variable. It’s always a good idea to remember which one is which! Anyway, what this does is create an “lm object” (i.e., a variable whose class is "lm") called regression_1. Let’s have a look at what happens when we print() it out:

print(regression_1)

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood)

Coefficients:

(Intercept) danielle_sleep 125.956 -8.937

[exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1003_v2] Learning Statistics with R — Statistical tools › 15 Linear regression › 15.3 Multiple linear regression › 15.3.1 Doing it in R (pages 612)
roles: formal, worked_example | topics: multiple-regression, linear-regression, estimation
teaches: Fits a two-predictor regression in R with lm, explains the implicit intercept, prints coefficients for danielle_sleep and baby_sleep, and interprets their relative sizes in the grumpiness example.
scope: R-specific multiple linear regression using danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep. The coefficient comments apply to this fitted parenthood model. The mentioned 3D regression-plane visualization is in excerpt 1004.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1004_v2
Multiple regression in R is no different to simple regression: all we have to do is specify a more complicated formula when using the lm() function. For example, if we want to use both danielle_sleep and baby_sleep as predictors in our attempt to explain why I’m so grumpy, then the formula we need is this:

danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep

Notice that, just like last time, I haven’t explicitly included any reference to the intercept term in this formula; only the two predictor variables and the outcome. By default, the lm() function assumes that the model should include an intercept (though you can get rid of it if you want). In any case, I can create a new regression model – which I’ll call regression_2 – using the following command:

regression_2 <- lm( formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood

)

And just like last time, if we print() out this regression model we can see what the estimated regression coeﬀicients are:

print(regression_2)

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood)

Coefficients:

(Intercept) danielle_sleep baby_sleep 125.96557 -8.95025 0.01052

[exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1019_v2] Learning Statistics with R — Statistical tools › 15 Linear regression › 15.5 Hypothesis tests for regression models › 15.5.3 Running the hypothesis tests in R (pages 620)
roles: worked_example | topics: linear-regression, regression-diagnostics, hypothesis-tests
teaches: Runs summary() on an R multiple-regression model with danielle_sleep and baby_sleep, displaying residuals, coefficients, t tests, R-squared, and the model F test.
scope: R-specific multiple linear regression with two predictors. The excerpt displays output; the line-by-line interpretation and model comparison are in the next excerpt. Do not use it as a simple-regression example.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1020_v2
To compute all of the quantities that we have talked about so far, all you need to do is ask for a summary() of your regression model. Since I’ve been using regression_2 as my example, let’s do that:

summary(regression_2)

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood)

Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max

-11.0345 -2.2198 -0.4016 2.6775 11.7496 Coefficients:

Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)

(Intercept) 125.96557 3.04095 41.423 <2e-16 *** danielle_sleep -8.95025 0.55346 -16.172 <2e-16 *** baby_sleep 0.01052 0.27106 0.039 0.969

--Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.354 on 97 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.8161, Adjusted R-squared: 0.8123 F-statistic: 215.2 on 2 and 97 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16

The output that this command produces is pretty dense, but we’ve already discussed everything of interest in it, so what I’ll do is go through it line by line. The first line reminds us of what the actual regression model is:

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood)

[exc_0689cddaba206d_728_v4] Advanced High School Statistics — Chapter 5 › Regression Analysis › 5.3 Least squares regression › Section summary (pages 473)
roles: summary | topics: linear-regression, correlation, regression-diagnostics
teaches: Reviews least-squares fitting, y-hat = a + bx, R-squared, the sign of correlation, coefficient interpretation, and cautions about intercepts outside the observed range.
scope: Section review for simple regression. R-squared is described as explained response variation and does not give association direction; use slope or the scatterplot for the sign of r. The intercept may be unreasonable when x=0 is extrapolation or yields an impossible response.
• The simple linear regression model is ﬁt to the data by minimizing the sum of the squares of the residuals. Because of this, the resulting equation is often called the least-squares regression line (LSRL) and is calculated using technology. This regression line will pass through the point (¯x , y¯).
• We write the least squares regression line in the form: yˆ = a+bx. The slope b and the y-intercept a can be calculated using technology or identiﬁed from computer output.
• In simple linear regression, the square of the correlation coeﬃcient, R2, is called the coeﬃcient of determination. R2 is the proportion of variation in the response variable that is explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable.
• R2 is always between 0 and 1, inclusive, or between 0% and 100%, inclusive. R2 applies to any type of model, not just a linear model, and can be used to compare the ﬁt among various models. The higher the value of R2, the better the model “ﬁts” the data.
• The value of R2 is always positive and cannot tell us the direction of the association. If ﬁnding r based on R2, make sure to use either the scatterplot or the slope of the regression line to determine whether r =+ √R2 or − √R2.
• The coeﬃcients a and b of the least-squares regression line model (line of best ﬁt) are statistics because they are based on a sample of values.
• The slope b of the least-squares regression line can be interpreted as the predicted increase or decrease in the response variable y for a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable x.

[exc_45ecdb7da7734b_279_v3] Learning Statistics with jamovi: A Tutorial for Beginners in Statistical Analysis — Correlation and linear regression › 12.4 Estimating a linear regression model › 12.4.1 Linear regression in jamovi (pages 287)
roles: worked_example | topics: linear-regression, jamovi | figures: fig_45ecdb7da7734b_2224_v3, fig_45ecdb7da7734b_2225_v3
teaches: Fits a simple linear regression in jamovi with dani.grump as outcome and dani.sleep as the sole predictor, yielding intercept 125.96, slope -8.94, and fitted line Y-hat=125.96-8.94X.
scope: Jamovi-specific implementation using parenthood.csv. This is simple linear regression with one predictor and an intercept. The fitted numbers belong to that dataset and should not be used as a multiple-regression example or a general behavioral relationship.
To run my linear regression, open up the ‘Regression’ – ‘Linear Regression’ analysis in jamovi, using the parenthood.csv data file. Then specify dani.grump as the ‘Dependent Variable’ and dani.sleep as the variable entered in the ‘Covariates’ box. This gives the

results shown in Figure 12.13, showing an intercept 𝑏̂0 = 125.96 and the slope 𝑏̂1 = −8.94. In other words, the best fitting regression line that I plotted in Figure 12.12 has this formula:

𝑌𝑖̂ = 125.96 + (−8.94𝑋𝑖)

Figure 12.13. A jamovi screenshot showing a simple linear regression analysis

teaches: Interprets the R summary for a two-predictor regression: residual quartiles, coefficient estimates and t tests, N-K-1 degrees of freedom, the model F test, R-squared, and evidence for dropping baby_sleep.
scope: Interpretation is tied to the multiple-regression output in excerpt 1019. Its residual-quartile check is described as quick and rough, not a full diagnostics procedure. The conclusion that regression_1 is preferable applies to this example, where baby_sleep p=.969 and R-squared=.816.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1019_v2
You can see why this is handy, since it was a little while back when we actually created the regression_2 model, and so it’s nice to be reminded of what it was we were doing. The next part provides a quick summary of the residuals (i.e., the 𝜖𝑖 values), which can be convenient as a quick and dirty check that the model is okay. Remember, we did assume that these residuals were normally distributed, with mean 0. In particular it’s worth quickly checking to see if the median is close to zero, and to see if the first quartile is about the same size as the third quartile. If they look badly off, there’s a good chance that the assumptions of regression are violated. These ones look pretty nice to me, so let’s move on to the interesting stuff. The next part of the R output looks at the coeﬀicients of the regression model. Each row in this table refers to one of the coeﬀicients in the regression model. The first row is the intercept term, and the later ones look at each of the predictors. The columns give you all of the relevant information. The first column is the actual estimate of 𝑏 (e.g., 125.96 for the intercept, and -8.9 for the danielle_sleep predictor). The second column is the standard error estimate 𝜎̂𝑏. The third column gives you the 𝑡-statistic, and it’s worth noticing that in this table 𝑡 = 𝑏/̂ SE(𝑏)̂ every time.

roles: introduction, formal, worked_example, exercise | topics: linear-regression, hypothesis-tests, t-tests | figures: fig_f213361bf057b0_5401_v3, fig_f213361bf057b0_5423_v3
Scope not reviewed. Check the source's applicability before using it.
Just like other point estimates we have seen before, we can compute a standard error and test statistic for b1. We will generally label the test statistic using a T, since it follows the t-distribution.

We will rely on statistical software to compute the standard error and leave the explanation of how this standard error is determined to a second or third statistics course. Figure 8.20 shows software output for the least squares regression line in Figure 8.19. The row labeled unemp includes the point estimate and other hypothesis test information for the slope, which is the coeﬃcient of the unemployment variable.

Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) -7.3644 5.1553 -1.43 0.1646 unemp -0.8897 0.8350 -1.07 0.2961 df = 27

Figure 8.20: Output from statistical software for the regression line modeling the midterm election losses for the President’s party as a response to unemployment.

EXAMPLE 8.19 START Example problem: What do the ﬁrst and second columns of Figure 8.20 represent?

Solution to the example: The entries in the ﬁrst column represent the least squares estimates, b0 and b1, and the values in the second column correspond to the standard errors of each estimate. Using the estimates, we could write the equation for the least square regression line as

yˆ = −7.3644 − 0.8897x

where yˆ in this case represents the predicted change in the number of seats for the president’s party, and x represents the unemployment rate.

EXAMPLE 8.19 HAS ENDED.

[exc_0689cddaba206d_710_v4] Advanced High School Statistics — Chapter 5 › Regression Analysis › 5.3 Least squares regression › 5.3.4 Using R2 to describe the strength of a ﬁt › Consider the scatterplot of gift aid versus family income for the Elmhurst College data, graphed in Figure 5.21. How well does the solid regression line ﬁt the data? And how much better is it than the horizontal dashed line at y¯ at ﬁtting the data? (pages 462, 463)
roles: introduction, formal, worked_example | topics: linear-regression, regression-diagnostics, correlation | figures: fig_0689cddaba206d_6339_v4, fig_0689cddaba206d_6355_v4, fig_0689cddaba206d_6356_v4, fig_0689cddaba206d_6358_v4
Scope not reviewed. Check the source's applicability before using it.
If we used the simple standard deviation of the residuals (dividing by n − 1 instead of n − 2), this would be exactly R2. For large data sets, this gives values suﬃciently close; however, to get the exact value of R2 we use a sum of squares method, which is described here in general terms.

Recall that we calculate a residual (y −yˆ) to see how well a regression line predicts a particular y-value. To measure how well the regression line ﬁts all the data, we need to calculate all of the residuals. We saw in the previous section that the sum of squared residuals is a way of measuring overall error about a line. In fact, the sum of squared errors about the regression line is smaller than about any other line. How much smaller is this sum than the sum of squared error about the line y¯? Note that we if we do not know x, our best prediction of y is simply y¯. In a sense, we are asking how much information using x and the regression line provides over ignoring x all together.

Let us take two extreme examples. In Figure 5.22(a), the correlation coeﬃcient is 0 and the regression line is the same as the horizontal line at y¯; the sum of the squared error about yˆ is equal to the sum of the squared error about y¯. R2 = 0: the regression line oﬀers no reduction in error; it “explains” 0% of the variation in the y points.

At this stage however, there’s really only two of them that you care about, and as it turns out you’ve seen them before:

However, more complicated formulas are allowed, and we’ll discuss them later.

teaches: Reviews least-squares fitting, y-hat = a + bx, R-squared, the sign of correlation, coefficient interpretation, and cautions about intercepts outside the observed range.
scope: Section review for simple regression. R-squared is described as explained response variation and does not give association direction; use slope or the scatterplot for the sign of r. The intercept may be unreasonable when x=0 is extrapolation or yields an impossible response.
chunks 1203-1204 of this excerpt, from 0

Full reviewed notes: Summarizes least-squares regression: the line minimizes squared residuals and passes through (x̄, ȳ); form ŷ = a + bx; R² is the proportion of variation in the response explained by the linear relationship, ranges 0 to 1, and does not indicate direction; a and b are sample statistics; slope b is the predicted change in y per one-unit increase in x; intercept a is the predicted y at x = 0, sometimes unreasonable due to extrapolation or impossible values; interpret a, b, and R² in context.

(chunk 1203) • The simple linear regression model is ﬁt to the data by minimizing the sum of the squares of the residuals. Because of this, the resulting equation is often called the least-squares regression line (LSRL) and is calculated using technology. This regression line will pass through the point (¯x , y¯).
• We write the least squares regression line in the form: yˆ = a+bx. The slope b and the y-intercept a can be calculated using technology or identiﬁed from computer output.
• In simple linear regression, the square of the correlation coeﬃcient, R2, is called the coeﬃcient of determination. R2 is the proportion of variation in the response variable that is explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable.
• R2 is always between 0 and 1, inclusive, or between 0% and 100%, inclusive. R2 applies to any type of model, not just a linear model, and can be used to compare the ﬁt among various models. The higher the value of R2, the better the model “ﬁts” the data.
• The value of R2 is always positive and cannot tell us the direction of the association. If ﬁnding r based on R2, make sure to use either the scatterplot or the slope of the regression line to determine whether r =+ √R2 or − √R2.
• The coeﬃcients a and b of the least-squares regression line model (line of best ﬁt) are statistics because they are based on a sample of values.
• The slope b of the least-squares regression line can be interpreted as the predicted increase or decrease in the response variable y for a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable x.

(chunk 1204) • The y-intercept a in the least-squares regression line is the predicted value of the response variable y when the explanatory variable x is equal to 0. Sometimes, the y-intercept of the line does not have a reasonable interpretation in context because x = 0 might be beyond the interval of x-values used to determine the regression line (extrapolation). At other times, the y-intercept of the line does not have a logical interpretation in context because it might be a negative value for a response variable that has no negative values, such as height.
• When interpreting a, b, and R2, always interpret them based on the situation, referencing the relevant variables in context.

(end of excerpt)

title: Simple Linear Regression in R with lm(): Fit and Interpret
content:
# Fitting and Interpreting Simple Linear Regression in R with `lm()`

## 1. Fitting the model

`lm()` takes two key arguments:

- **`formula`** — the model, written `outcome ~ predictor` (outcome on the left, predictor on the right). The intercept is included by default; you never type it.
- **`data`** — the data frame containing the variables.

The output is a complicated "lm object", so store it in a variable:

```r
regression_1 <- lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood)
```

Here `danielle_grump` is the outcome and `danielle_sleep` the predictor — always keep track of which is which.

## 2. Quick look: `print()`

```r
print(regression_1)
```
```
Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood)
Coefficients:
(Intercept)  danielle_sleep
    125.956          -8.937
```

This gives just the fitted coefficients: ŷ = 125.956 − 8.937·x.

## 3. Full output: `summary()`

```r
summary(regression_1)
```

The summary is dense but every part is useful:

- **Call** — reminds you which model you fitted.
- **Residuals** — Min, 1Q, Median, 3Q, Max. A quick-and-rough check: the median should be near 0 and the 1st and 3rd quartiles roughly symmetric in size; badly off values suggest the regression assumptions are violated.
- **Coefficients table** — one row per coefficient (intercept first, then each predictor). Columns:
  - `Estimate`: the fitted coefficient b̂ (e.g., intercept 125.96, slope −8.9).
  - `Std. Error`: the standard error of that estimate.
  - `t value`: the t-statistic, and note that t = b̂ / SE(b̂) every time.
  - `Pr(>|t|)`: the p-value for the test that the coefficient is zero, with significance stars (`***` p < 0.001, `**` p < 0.01, `*` p < 0.05, `.` p < 0.1).
- **Residual standard error** — typical size of the residuals, with degrees of freedom (N − K − 1).
- **Multiple R-squared / Adjusted R-squared** — model fit.
- **F-statistic** — overall test that the model (all predictors jointly) explains the outcome.

## 4. Interpreting the coefficients

- **Slope (b₁)**: the predicted change in the response for a one-unit increase in the predictor. In the example, each extra hour of sleep predicts about 8.9 fewer grumpiness points. The slope's sign gives the direction of the association.
- **Intercept (b₀)**: the predicted response when the predictor equals 0. Be careful: if x = 0 is outside the observed data range (extrapolation) or gives an impossible response (e.g., negative height), the intercept may not be meaningful in context even though it is needed for the line.
- The coefficients are **statistics** — estimates from a sample — so the standard errors, t statistics and p-values tell you how much uncertainty surrounds them.
- Always interpret a, b and R² in context, referencing the actual variables.

## 5. Interpreting R²

- R² is the **coefficient of determination**: the proportion of variation in the response explained by the linear relationship with the predictor. It ranges from 0 to 1 (0%–100%); higher = better fit.
- R² is always positive and **cannot tell you the direction** of the association — use the slope or the scatterplot for that (r = ±√R²).
- R² applies to any type of model and can be used to compare fits among models.

## Worked example (parenthood data)

Fitting `danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep` gives intercept 125.96 and slope −8.94, so the fitted line is ŷ = 125.96 − 8.94·x. The slope is highly significant (tiny p-value), and the model's R² is large, meaning most of the variation in grumpiness is explained by sleep. (The full `summary()` output shown in the source is for the two-predictor extension of this model; the simple-regression summary has the same structure with one predictor row.)

*Scope note: this note covers R's `lm()` for simple linear regression (one predictor plus intercept). Multiple regression uses the same functions with a longer formula, but its interpretation details are not covered here.*
